topics.title: After the Mauryas: new kingdoms in India

learn.hook: When a huge empire breaks up, many new kingdoms rise to fill the space. That's what happened after the Mauryas.
points: Around 185 BCE, the last Mauryan ruler, Bṛihadratha, was overthrown by his general Pushyamitra Shunga, who started the Shunga dynasty. The Kāṇvas later followed the Shungas.

In the Deccan, the Sātavāhanas became powerful. Their capital was Pratiṣhṭhāna (Paithan) on the Godavari. Many Sātavāhana kings were named after their mothers, such as Gautamīputra Sātakarṇi, 'son of Gautamī'.
In Kalinga, King Khāravela became powerful some time after the Mauryas. His Hāthīgumphā inscription in the Udayagiri hills near Bhubaneswar records his deeds; he was a follower of Jainism.
In the far south, the Cheras, Cholas and Pāṇḍyas ruled Tamilakam. Early Tamil poems called Sangam literature describe their kings, poets, farmers and ports.
Historians call this period an 'age of reorganisation' because power was divided among many kingdoms, while trade and culture kept growing.

example.q: The king's name 'Gautamīputra Sātakarṇi' tells us something. What does 'Gautamīputra' show?
steps: 'Gautamī' is the name of his mother.
So the king was known as the son of Gautamī.
example.answer: It shows that Sātavāhana kings were often named after their mothers.

learn.reallife: The Hāthīgumphā ('elephant cave') inscription and the Udayagiri–Khandagiri caves near Bhubaneswar can still be visited today.

quiz.q: Who founded the Shunga dynasty?
quiz.explain: Pushyamitra, a Mauryan general, overthrew Bṛihadratha around 185 BCE.
quiz.mistake: Confuses rulers of different regions

quiz.q: The Sātavāhanas ruled mainly in:
quiz.explain: Their kingdom was in the Deccan, with Pratiṣhṭhāna on the Godavari as a capital.
quiz.mistake: Does not place the Sātavāhanas on the map

quiz.q: What is unusual about names like Gautamīputra Sātakarṇi?
options: The king is named after his mother
The name is of a river
quiz.explain: Gautamīputra means 'son of Gautamī', his mother.
quiz.mistake: Assumes ancient kings were named only after fathers

quiz.q: Khāravela's deeds are recorded in the:
quiz.explain: The Hāthīgumphā inscription is in the Udayagiri hills near Bhubaneswar.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up famous inscriptions

quiz.q: Which faith did Khāravela follow?
quiz.explain: Khāravela was a follower of Jainism and supported Jain monks.
quiz.mistake: Does not know about Khāravela's faith

quiz.q: Which three kingdoms ruled Tamilakam in this period?
quiz.explain: The 'three crowned kings' of the Tamil region were the Cheras, Cholas and Pāṇḍyas.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up northern and southern dynasties

quiz.q: Sangam literature is written in:
quiz.explain: Sangam poems are among the oldest works of Tamil literature.
quiz.mistake: Assumes all early texts were in Sanskrit

quiz.q: Why is this period called an 'age of reorganisation'?
options: One empire ruled all of Asia
Power was shared among many new kingdoms after the Mauryan Empire
quiz.explain: After the Mauryas, many kingdoms rose in different regions while trade and culture went on.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the period was one of collapse with nothing new

teach.ask: Gappu wonders what happened after the Mauryan Empire ended. Tell him about the new kingdoms.
teach.praise: Shungas, Sātavāhanas, Khāravela and the Tamil kings. So many new kingdoms!
teach.nudge: Good! And who ruled in the Deccan, or in the far south?

learn.hook: Greek kings who discussed Buddhism, and Central Asian rulers who issued gold coins: north-west India was a meeting place of peoples.
points: Indo-Greek kings ruled parts of the north-west. The most famous, Menander (Milinda), is remembered in a Buddhist text, the Milinda-pañha ('Questions of Milinda'), where he asks the monk Nāgasena about the Buddha's teachings.
Heliodorus, a Greek ambassador, set up a pillar at Besnagar near Vidisha in honour of Vāsudeva (Krishna).
The Shakas came from Central Asia. The Shaka ruler Rudradāman's inscription at Junagadh (Girnar), in Sanskrit, records the repair of the Sudarshana lake.
The Kushānas built a large kingdom; their greatest ruler, Kanishka, supported Buddhism. Their capitals included Puruṣhapura (Peshawar) and Mathurā.
Many newcomers adopted Indian names, languages and faiths, and became part of Indian society.

example.q: A Greek ambassador set up a pillar honouring an Indian deity. What does this tell us about the time?
steps: Heliodorus came from a Greek kingdom, yet he honoured Vāsudeva.
This shows that newcomers were adopting Indian beliefs.
It suggests the period was one of mixing and exchange of cultures.
example.answer: That people from outside were becoming part of Indian culture and faith.

learn.reallife: The Government Museum in Mathura displays a Kushāna-period statue of Kanishka.

games.title: Who's who?
pairs: Greek ambassador who set up a pillar at Besnagar
Shaka ruler of the Junagadh inscription
Great Kushāna ruler who supported Buddhism

games.title: True or false: newcomers
items: The Milinda-pañha records questions asked by King Menander.
He discusses the Buddha's teachings with the monk Nāgasena.
Rudradāman's Junagadh inscription is in Sanskrit.
It is one of the early long inscriptions in Sanskrit.
Kanishka was a Sātavāhana king of the Deccan.
Kanishka was a Kushāna ruler in the north and north-west.
Many newcomers adopted Indian names and faiths.
Heliodorus and many others joined Indian traditions.
The Shakas came from Central Asia.
They were Central Asian peoples who settled in western and northern India.

quiz.q: Which Indo-Greek king is remembered in the Milinda-pañha?
quiz.explain: Menander, called Milinda in Indian texts, asks the monk Nāgasena about Buddhism.
quiz.mistake: Confuses Menander with Alexander

quiz.q: The monk who answered Milinda's questions was:
quiz.explain: Nāgasena is the Buddhist monk in the Milinda-pañha.
quiz.mistake: Picks another famous name from ancient times

quiz.q: Heliodorus set up his pillar in honour of:
quiz.explain: The Besnagar pillar honours Vāsudeva, showing a Greek adopting an Indian faith.
quiz.mistake: Assumes a Greek would honour a Greek god

quiz.q: Rudradāman was a ruler of the:
quiz.explain: Rudradāman was a famous Shaka ruler in western India.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the Shakas and the Kushānas

quiz.q: Rudradāman's Junagadh inscription records the repair of:
options: A Buddhist stupa in Sri Lanka
quiz.explain: It describes how the Sudarshana lake, a reservoir, was repaired.
quiz.mistake: Does not know what the inscription records

quiz.q: Who was the greatest Kushāna ruler?
quiz.explain: Kanishka ruled a large Kushāna kingdom and supported Buddhism.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up rulers from different dynasties

quiz.q: Puruṣhapura, a Kushāna capital, is today's:
quiz.explain: Puruṣhapura is modern Peshawar.
quiz.mistake: Guesses from the similar first letter

quiz.q: What does the story of the newcomers show about Indian society at this time?
options: Outsiders were never allowed to settle
Many outsiders adopted Indian ways and became part of it
quiz.explain: Greeks, Shakas and Kushānas took Indian names, languages and faiths.
quiz.mistake: Thinks cultures only clashed and never mixed

teach.ask: Gappu asks who came into India from the north-west in this age, and what happened to them.
teach.praise: Greeks, Shakas and Kushānas came and many became part of Indian life. What a mix!
teach.nudge: You named the newcomers. Did they stay outsiders, or did they mix with Indian culture?

learn.hook: Indian pepper was so valued by Roman traders that it is often called 'black gold'. Ships crossed the ocean to buy it!
points: Trade grew by land and sea. The Silk Route linked China, Central Asia, India and the Mediterranean world; Kushāna rule helped trade along these routes.
Traders used the monsoon winds to sail across the Arabian Sea. Spices (especially pepper), cotton cloth, gems and ivory went west.
Roman coins have been found in south India, and Arikamedu near Puducherry was an important trading site. Muziris on the Kerala coast was a famous port.
Art flourished. Gandhāra art, influenced by Greek styles, made Buddha images with wavy hair and flowing robes; Mathurā art used local red sandstone.
The gateways (toraṇas) of the Great Stupa at Sanchi, with their beautiful carvings, belong largely to this age. Sanskrit, Prakrit and Tamil literature also flourished.

example.q: Many Roman gold and silver coins have been dug up in Tamil Nadu and Kerala. What does this tell historians?
steps: Roman traders must have paid for goods with these coins.
So there was active trade between south India and the Roman world.
The goods they bought were mainly spices, cloth and gems.
example.answer: That south India had busy sea trade with the Roman world.

learn.reallife: Kerala is still one of India's major pepper-growing regions, carrying on a spice trade that is over 2,000 years old.

games.title: Gandhāra or Mathurā art?
items: Local Indian style near the Yamuna

items.text: Indian ___ was so valued that it was called black gold.
Sailors used the ___ winds to cross the Arabian Sea.
___ near Puducherry was an important trading site.
The carved gateways of a stupa are called ___.

quiz.q: Which spice from India was so valued that it was called 'black gold'?
quiz.explain: Black pepper from the Malabar coast was in huge demand in the Roman world.
quiz.mistake: Picks another Indian spice

quiz.q: The Silk Route linked:
options: China, Central Asia, India and the Mediterranean
quiz.explain: The Silk Route was a network of land routes across Asia to the Mediterranean.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the route was only inside India

quiz.q: Why have Roman coins been found in south India?
options: Indians made Roman coins for fun
Romans paid for Indian goods like spices and cloth
They fell from ships by accident only
quiz.explain: The coins show active trade between south India and the Roman world.
quiz.mistake: Thinks coins prove conquest rather than trade

quiz.q: Which ancient trading site is near Puducherry?
quiz.explain: Arikamedu was an ancient port-town where Roman pottery has been found.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up trading sites with Buddhist sites

quiz.q: How did ancient sailors use the monsoon?
options: Seasonal winds helped them sail across the sea
It stopped all sea travel forever
It pushed ships only up rivers
quiz.explain: Knowing when the winds changed direction let ships sail to and from India.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the monsoon is only about rain

quiz.q: Gandhāra art is known for:
quiz.explain: Gandhāra sculptors mixed Greek styles with Buddhist themes.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up Gandhāra art with later southern art

quiz.q: Mathurā sculptures were mostly made of:
quiz.explain: The Mathurā school used the local red sandstone.
quiz.mistake: Thinks all ancient sculpture was marble

quiz.q: The carved gateways at the Great Stupa of Sanchi are called:
quiz.explain: Toraṇas are the decorated gateways around the stupa.
quiz.mistake: Uses the name of a different kind of structure

teach.ask: Gappu asks what was being traded in this age and what art was made. Explain to him.
teach.praise: Pepper to Rome, coins back to India, and beautiful art at Gandhāra, Mathurā and Sanchi. What a busy time!
teach.nudge: You talked about trade. What kinds of art and sculpture were made?
